newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul trade balance improves for 4th month in row.
newsitem.headline: Seoul trade balance improves for 4th month in row.

text.p: South Korea's trade balance improved for the fourth consecutive month in July when the deficit more than halved due to the won's weakness and brisk semiconductor exports, the trade ministry said on Friday.
The ministry said the customs-cleared trade deficit fell to a provisional $806 million in July from a $2.83 billion shortfall a year earlier.
In June, the country posted its first monthly trade surplus in 30 months with $44 million versus a $426 million deficit in June 1996.
The trade deficit for the first seven months of this year also shrank to $9.95 billion from a $10.91 billion shortfall during the same seven-month period in 1996.

"Exports rose sharply due to improving price competitiveness following the won's depreciation, stable local product prices and wages and stable growth in the world economy and trade," a ministry report said.
It put the won's value against the U.S. dollar at an average of 865.3 for this year, down 10.8 percent from an average of 771.0 recorded in 1995. The won continued to weaken in 1996.

Semiconductor exports rose 36.6 percent on the year to $1.5 billion in July mainly due to an increased demand for 64-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips, non-memory chips and assembled items, it said.

Falling prices of 16-megabit DRAMs, the mainstay among computer memory chips, had only limited impact on the nation's overall semiconductor exports due to the declining proportion of the item in overall semiconductor exports, it said.
The unit price for 16-megabit DRAM chip exports fell to $8.0 in July, compared with $9.5 in March and $8.5 at the end of 1996, the report said.
A plunge of about 80 percent in 16-megabit DRAM prices has widely been blamed for the sharp expansion in the nation's annual trade deficit in 1996.
Last year, South Korea's trade deficit more than doubled to a record $20.62 billion from $10.06 billion in 1995.
The report said automobile exports for the first 20 days of July rose by a strong 22.7 percent from a year earlier despite the financial troubles at the Kia Group.
"But the nation's automobile exports are feared to be damaged by the group's troubles unless they are settled quickly," said the report.
The two automaking units of the Kia Group, Kia Motors Corp and Asia Motors Corp, together accounted for 31 percent of the nation's automobile exports for the first half of this year, it said.
Kia, the nation's eighth-largest conglomerate, has run into financial troubles mainly because of a local sales slump suffered by its two automaking units.
Kia's creditor banks on July 15 selected 18 of Kia's 38 affiliates for bail-out under their voluntary scheme formed in April to prevent promising companies from folding.

The report said impact from recent currency devaluations in Thailand and the Philippines would be relatively small in view of the weak proportion of South Korean exports to the two Southeast Asian nations.
